svg.title: Case 3: an unverifiable business case lost phase two funding, and the measurable table that won it back
svg.desc: The red band at the top quotes the original business case, improve the overall security level, with eight million spent and no visible change, so phase two was rejected. Three metric rows then carry the table that replaced it: mean time to detect a compromised host fell from 21 days to 4 hours through NetFlow and centralised logging, mean time to repair fell from 5 days to 6 hours through automated isolation playbooks, and non-compliant endpoint connection events fell from more than 30 a month to 2 through NAC with posture checks. A green band states that phase two was approved because the CIO could put this table in front of the board, and a closing note explains that MTTD depends on visibility while MTTR depends on resilience and automation.
svg.text: Case 3: “improve the overall security level” is not a business case
Eight million spent, nothing countable to show, phase two refused — and the same project rescued by three rows of a table
The business case that failed: 8M on firewalls, microsegmentation and NAC, justified by “improve the overall security level” — not specific, not measurable.
What the CIO saw was eight million spent and no visible change, so the phase-two request was rejected.
MTTD · mean time to find a compromised host
detection is a data problem before it is a tool problem
same team, the recovery finally written down
the only row a board member repeats verbatim
Phase two was approved — not because the second proposal was better engineered, but because the CIO could put this table in front of the board.
MTTD depends on visibility, MTTR on resilience and automation: naming them on Day 0 locks the technical direction before the first purchase order.
